2.definition: The long-Romanized native population of the Iberian Peninsula — descendants of the people Rome had governed for six centuries, mostly Catholic Christians speaking a Latin that was already drifting toward Spanish.
Arabic for "Tariq's mountain," named for the Berber commander Tariq ibn Ziyad who landed beneath it in 711. Eight centuries of European mangling turned the name into "Gibraltar."

3.definition: The thughur were the fortified frontier marches of the Islamic world — chains of garrison towns and border fortresses guarding the edge of Muslim territory, most famously the war-zone facing the Byzantine Empire.

6.definition: The book collections kept by monasteries in Christian western Europe. Around the year 970 even an impressive one held only a few hundred hand-copied manuscripts — a fraction of what the great libraries of al-Andalus contained.

Worshipping and conducting its liturgy in Greek rather than Latin. The Byzantine (Eastern) church used Greek as its sacred and administrative language, one of the deep markers separating it from the Latin-speaking Western church that answered to the Pope in Rome.

8.definition: A burst of flourishing in learning, art, and ideas. The point al-Andalus makes is that it can happen even when a region is politically fragmented — splintered power and cultural brilliance aren't opposites.

9.definition: Arabic for "the lord" or "the master" (al-sayyid). It is the title that Rodrigo Díaz's Muslim contemporaries gave him, which Christian Spain reworked into his immortal nickname, El Cid.
Of Castile, the central and ultimately dominant Christian kingdom of medieval Iberia — the power whose language became modern Spanish and whose monarchs completed the Reconquista.

10.definition: An Arabic honorific laqab meaning "the Victorious," adopted as a regnal title by Muslim rulers who wished to advertise a military triumph. Here it is the victory-name taken by the Almohad caliph Abu Yusuf Yaqub after Alarcos — the same boast Almanzor of Cordoba had claimed two centuries earlier, with no connection between the men beyond the title.

13.definition: Andrew Watson was an economic historian best known for his 1970s thesis that early Islamic rule spread a wave of new crops and irrigation across the Mediterranean — the so-called 'Arab Agricultural Revolution.'

A universal version of the astrolabe, the handheld brass instrument of the medieval sky. Refined by the Toledo astronomer Arzachel, it worked at any latitude rather than needing a different plate for each location.

14.definition: The honorific the medieval Latin schoolmen gave Averroes — capital C, no name needed — just as Aristotle was simply "the Philosopher." It marks how completely his commentaries dominated Europe's reading of Aristotle.

16.definition: The adjectival form of Castile — meaning belonging to or under the Crown of Castile, the dominant Christian kingdom of central Iberia to which Nasrid Granada paid tribute and owed military service.

17.definition: Of Castile, the central and ultimately dominant Christian kingdom of medieval Iberia — the power whose language became modern Spanish and whose monarchs completed the Reconquista.

18.definition: Of or relating to al-Andalus — the Muslim-ruled portion of medieval Iberia and its culture. The "Andalusian paradise" is the romanticized image of that lost society as a golden age of tolerance and learning.
